background:
Titus: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

Titus is a short letter of instructions to Paul's co-worker Titus, whom he left on Crete to appoint elders and correct false teaching. It stresses that sound teaching must produce “good works.” Traditionally it dates to about AD 63–65, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul (1:1)One of the Pastoral Letters; the traditional view holds Paul wrote it, though many scholars think a follower did.
DateAbout AD 63–65After Paul's release from house arrest in Rome; Acts does not describe a mission on Crete.
Written fromUnknown; perhaps Macedonia or GreecePaul planned to spend the winter at Nicopolis on the west coast of Greece (3:12).
RecipientTitus, a Gentile believerPaul's trusted troubleshooter, who had handled the delicate situation in Corinth (2 Cor 7–8) and was a test case for Gentile freedom (Gal 2:3).
SituationYoung churches in many towns needing leadersTitus was to appoint elders “in every city” (1:5) and silence “vain talkers,” especially “they of the circumcision” (1:10).
Key word“Good works,” six timesGrace saves (3:5) and grace trains believers to live godly lives (2:11–12).

Two great summaries of the gospel (2:11–14 and 3:4–7) anchor the letter's practical instructions.

The time map

The shaded band marks the traditional date, AD 62–65, after Paul's release and before Nero's persecution and his final arrest.

Rome and the province of Crete

Crete had been conquered by Rome in 67 BC and was governed together with Cyrene in North Africa.

  • A Roman province. Crete and Cyrene formed a single province, with its capital at Gortyn in southern Crete, where Roman buildings and a famous law code inscription can still be seen.
  • A famous insult. Paul quotes a Cretan prophet: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons” (1:12). The line is credited to the poet Epimenides of Knossos (about 600 BC); Greeks used “to cretize” to mean “to lie.”
  • Jews on Crete. Cretans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), and Josephus mentions a Jewish community on the island. The false teachers included Jewish believers pressing myths and rules (1:10, 14).
  • Households. Paul's instructions to older and younger men and women, and slaves (2:1–10), follow common Roman household patterns, but the aim is “that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour.”
  • Saviors and epiphanies. Emperors were hailed as saviors whose appearance (epiphaneia) brought blessings. Paul speaks of the grace of God that “hath appeared” and the “appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (2:11, 13).
  • Submission to rulers. Believers should be subject to rulers and ready for every good work (3:1), commending the gospel through good citizenship.

Nero was emperor; within a few years Rome would turn on the Christians, making the call to blameless, peaceable living all the more important.

Crete and Nicopolis

Crete is the largest Greek island, about 160 miles long, with many small towns in its valleys and along its coasts.

  • Paul on Crete. Paul's ship stopped at Fair Havens on Crete on the way to Rome (Acts 27:7–13). Titus 1:5 implies a later mission there, after Acts.
  • Many towns. Crete had dozens of independent towns, which is why Titus had to appoint elders “in every city.”
  • Knossos. Home of the ancient Minoan palace and of Epimenides, whose saying Paul quotes.
  • Nicopolis. “Victory City,” founded by Augustus to celebrate his victory at Actium in 31 BC, on the west coast of Greece. Paul planned to winter there (3:12).
  • Zenas and Apollos. Titus is asked to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey (3:13), probably the travelers who carried the letter.
  • Titus later. 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus went to Dalmatia; church tradition remembers him as the first bishop of Crete.

Around the world in the early 60s

Titus was written in a tense decade for the Roman world.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainBoudica's revolt (AD 60–61). The queen of the Iceni burned London, Colchester and St Albans before being crushed.
RomeNero's early good years ended about AD 62. The Great Fire of AD 64 was followed by the first persecution of Christians.
JudeaTension grew; James the Lord's brother was killed in AD 62. The Jewish revolt broke out in AD 66.
Armenia and ParthiaA compromise peace in AD 63; Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
ItalyAn earthquake damaged Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 62, seventeen years before Vesuvius buried them.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming; silk reached Rome along the trade routes.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire was forming in the northwest; tradition says Thomas preached in India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was growing; the Moche and Nazca cultures flourished in Peru.

How the setting shapes the study

Several phrases in Titus come alive in its setting.

PassageConnection to the times
Titus 1:5Crete had many independent towns, each needing its own elders.
Titus 1:12The saying about Cretans comes from Epimenides of Knossos, about 600 BC.
Titus 1:14“Jewish fables”: speculative stories built on Scripture, as in Ephesus (1 Tim 1:4).
Titus 2:5“That the word of God be not blasphemed”: outsiders judged the church by its households.
Titus 2:9–10Many believers were slaves; faithful work could “adorn the doctrine.”
Titus 2:11–13Emperors' “appearances” were celebrated as bringing salvation; Paul points to Christ's.
Titus 3:1Believers should be subject to rulers and authorities, under Nero.
Titus 3:12Nicopolis was Augustus' victory city on the Greek west coast.
Titus 3:13Traveling Christians depended on churches for supplies and hospitality.

On an island known for its bad reputation, Paul expects grace to produce people “zealous of good works” (2:14).

Maps: then and now

Crete lies at the southern edge of the Aegean. Nicopolis, where Paul hoped to spend the winter, lay on the opposite side of Greece.

Today Crete is part of Greece, with about 600,000 people. The ruins of Gortyn and Nicopolis are open to visitors.

items.text: Greeting
Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s elect, and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness,
in hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before times eternal;
but in his own seasons manifested his word in the message, wherewith I was intrusted according to the commandment of God our Saviour;
to Titus, my true child after a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.
Qualifications for Elders
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that were wanting, and appoint elders in every city, as I gave thee charge;
if any man is blameless, the husband of one wife, having children that believe, who are not accused of riot or unruly.
For the bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward; not self-willed, not soon angry, no brawler, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre;
but given to hospitality, a lover of good, sober-minded, just, holy, self-controlled;
holding to the faithful word which is according to the teaching, that he may be able both to exhort in the sound doctrine, and to convict the gainsayers.
Rebuke False Teachers
For there are many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision,
whose mouths must be stopped; men who overthrow whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake.
One of themselves, a prophet of their own, said, Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons.
This testimony is true. For which cause reprove them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men who turn away from the truth.
To the pure all things are pure: but to them that are defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; but both their mind and their conscience are defiled.
They profess that they know God; but by their works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul greets Titus as a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, sent for the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, in hope of eternal life promised before times eternal. He left Titus in Crete to set things in order and appoint elders in every city.

An elder must be blameless, faithful in marriage, with believing and orderly children; not arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent or greedy, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, just and holy, holding firmly to the trustworthy word so he can encourage with sound doctrine and refute opponents. Many rebellious people, especially of the circumcision, are upsetting whole households for shameful gain. Even a Cretan prophet said Cretans are liars, so Titus must rebuke them sharply. “To the pure all things are pure,” but these people profess to know God while denying Him by their works.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What qualities does Paul require of elders in verses 5–9, and why must they hold fast the faithful word?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would Paul quote a Cretan prophet about Cretans (vv. 12–13), and what does this suggest about the culture Titus faced on Crete?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Some profess to know God but deny him by their works (v. 16); where might your words and actions be pulling in different directions?

items.text: Teach What Accords with Sound Doctrine
But speak thou the things which befit the sound doctrine:
that aged men be temperate, grave, sober-minded, sound in faith, in love, in patience:
that aged women likewise be reverent in demeanor, not slanderers nor enslaved to much wine, teachers of that which is good;
that they may train the young women to love their husbands, to love their children,
to be sober-minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, being in subjection to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed:
the younger men likewise exhort to be sober-minded:
in all things showing thyself an ensample of good works; in thy doctrine showing uncorruptness, gravity,
sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of us.
Exhort servants to be in subjection to their own masters, and to be well-pleasing to them in all things; not gainsaying;
not purloining, but showing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
The Grace of God Has Appeared
For the grace of God hath appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
instructing us, to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly and righteously and godly in this present world;
looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a people for his own possession, zealous of good works.
These things speak and exhort and reprove with all authority. Let no man despise thee.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Titus must teach what fits sound doctrine. Older men should be sober, dignified, self-controlled and sound in faith, love and patience. Older women should be reverent, not slanderers or slaves to wine, teaching what is good and training younger women to love their husbands and children and to be self-controlled and pure, “that the word of God be not blasphemed.” Younger men should be self-controlled, and Titus himself must be a model of good works and sound speech. Slaves should be faithful, “that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.”

The reason for all this: “the grace of God hath appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us, to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly and righteously and godly in this present world; looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ; who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a people for his own possession, zealous of good works.” Titus must teach these things with all authority.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What instructions are given to older men, older women, younger women and younger men in verses 2–6, and what does Titus himself model (vv. 7–8)?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why was Paul concerned that the word of God not be blasphemed (v. 5) by the household conduct of believers in a watching Roman society?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Grace is said to train us to live soberly, righteously and godly (vv. 11–12); how is God's grace teaching you something new about daily living?

items.text: Saved by God's Mercy
Put them in mind to be in subjection to rulers, to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready unto every good work,
to speak evil of no man, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all meekness toward all men.
For we also once were foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Saviour, and his love toward man, appeared,
not by works done in righteousness, which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit,
which he poured out upon us richly, through Jesus Christ our Saviour;
that, being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
Devote Yourselves to Good Works

Faithful is the saying, and concerning these things I desire that thou affirm confidently, to the end that they who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men:
but shun foolish questionings, and genealogies, and strifes, and fightings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
A factious man after a first and second admonition refuse;
knowing that such a one is perverted, and sinneth, being self-condemned.
Final Instructions and Greetings
When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, give diligence to come unto me to Nicopolis: for there I have determined to winter.
Set forward Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them.
And let our people also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.
All that are with me salute thee. Salute them that love us in faith. Grace be with you all.

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: Believers should be subject to rulers and authorities, ready for every good work, speaking evil of no one, gentle and showing meekness to all. For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient and enslaved to passions, hateful and hating one another. “But when the kindness of God our Saviour, and his love toward man, appeared, not by works done in righteousness, which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit,” so that, justified by His grace, we might become heirs of eternal life.

Titus must insist on these things so that believers will be careful to maintain good works. He should avoid foolish questions, genealogies and quarrels about the Law, and warn a divisive person once or twice before having nothing more to do with him. Paul plans to send Artemas or Tychicus and asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis for the winter, and to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way. Believers must learn to devote themselves to good works so they are not unfruitful.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: How does Paul describe our former life in verse 3 and God's saving kindness in verses 4–7?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would being subject to rulers and authorities and ready for every good work (v. 1) matter for Christians on Crete living under Roman governance?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul urges people to learn to maintain good works for necessary uses (v. 14); what practical need around you could your group meet together?

wrap.title: Titus In Summary
paras: Titus is a practical letter to a church planter on a difficult assignment. Paul had left Titus on Crete, an island with many young churches, a reputation for dishonesty and a group of false teachers upsetting households for profit. Paul tells Titus to appoint trustworthy elders, silence the troublemakers and teach believers how to live.

The letter's repeated theme is that true doctrine produces good lives. Paul uses the phrase “good works” six times. The false teachers profess to know God but deny Him by their actions; genuine believers, by contrast, should adorn the teaching of God our Savior by the way they live, so that outsiders have nothing bad to say.

Paul gives instructions for every group in the church: elders, older men and women, younger men and women, Titus himself and slaves. These are ordinary virtues (self-control, faithfulness, kindness, honesty), but they are rooted in the gospel, and they make the gospel attractive to a watching world.

Two beautiful summaries of the gospel stand at the center. In 2:11–14 the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation and training us to live godly lives as we wait for the appearing of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. In 3:4–7 God saved us not because of our works but by His mercy, through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, so that we are justified by grace and become heirs of eternal life.
The message in one line: God saves us by His grace and mercy alone, and the same grace trains us to live sober, godly and generous lives that adorn the gospel in a skeptical world.
